toolRandom.aboutContent:
What Is the Random Palette Generator?

The Random Palette Generator is a free online tool that instantly creates harmonious five-color palettes based on proven color theory principles. Whether you are a graphic designer searching for fresh inspiration, a web developer prototyping a new interface, or an artist exploring unexpected color combinations, this tool delivers curated results in a single click.

Unlike simple random-color pickers, our generator applies harmony rules — monochromatic, analogous, complementary, triadic, and tetradic — so every palette feels balanced and intentional. Each color comes with its HEX, RGB, and HSL values, ready to paste directly into your CSS, design file, or illustration software.

Real-world use cases include branding mood boards, social-media graphics, presentation slides, interior-design explorations, and creative warm-up exercises. Because the palettes are algorithmically balanced, they serve as an excellent starting point that you can fine-tune to your project's unique requirements.

  • Ideal for designers, developers, marketers, and hobbyists
  • No sign-up required — completely free
  • Works on desktop and mobile browsers
toolRandom.howToContent:
How to Use the Random Palette Generator

Getting a beautiful palette takes only seconds. Follow these steps to generate, customize, and export your colors.

  1. Open the tool — Navigate to the Random Palette Generator page. A five-color palette is displayed automatically.
  2. Generate a new palette — Press the Spacebar on your keyboard or click the Generate New Palette button. A fresh set of harmonious colors appears instantly.
  3. Lock colors you like — Click the lock icon on any color swatch to keep it fixed. The next generation will randomize only the unlocked colors, letting you build around a favorite shade.
  4. Copy individual colors — Click a color code (HEX, RGB, or HSL) to copy it to your clipboard for immediate use in your project.
  5. Export the full palette — Use the export menu to download the palette as CSS variables, Tailwind config, SCSS variables, JSON, PNG, or SVG.
  6. Save to history — Every palette you generate is saved in your local browser history, so you can revisit and restore past favorites at any time.

Tip: combine this tool with the Contrast Checker to verify that your generated colors meet WCAG accessibility standards before shipping a design.

toolColor.aboutContent:
What Is the Color Harmony Explorer?

The Color Harmony Explorer is a free online tool that takes a single base color and generates complete palettes using classic color-theory harmony rules. It is the fastest way to move from a single brand color or inspiration shade to a full, balanced palette ready for design work.

Color harmony is the foundation of effective visual communication. When colors are related through mathematical relationships on the color wheel — such as complementary (opposite), analogous (adjacent), triadic (evenly spaced), or monochromatic (same hue, different lightness) — they create a sense of order and aesthetic pleasure that resonates with viewers.

This tool is invaluable for brand designers defining primary and secondary palettes, UI/UX designers building design systems, illustrators planning color scripts, and marketers creating on-brand social content. Simply pick your starting color and let the algorithms handle the rest.

  • Four harmony modes: Monochromatic, Analogous, Complementary, and Triadic
  • Instant palette generation from any base color
  • Perfect for brand guidelines and design systems
  • Copy individual colors or export the full palette
toolColor.howToContent:
How to Use the Color Harmony Explorer

Building a harmonious palette from a single color is straightforward. Follow these steps to discover beautiful combinations.

  1. Select a base color — Use the color picker or paste a HEX code into the Base Color input to set your starting point. This is typically your primary brand color or a color you drew from a photo.
  2. Choose a harmony mode — Click one of the four harmony tabs: Mono (monochromatic), Analogous, Comp (complementary), or Triadic. The palette updates instantly to reflect the chosen rule.
  3. Review the generated palette — Examine the five-color palette displayed below the controls. Each swatch shows its HEX value.
  4. Experiment with modes — Switch between harmony modes to compare results. Monochromatic gives a subtle, tonal feel; analogous offers warmth and cohesion; complementary delivers strong contrast; triadic provides vibrant variety.
  5. Copy colors — Click any swatch or code to copy it to your clipboard.
  6. Export — Use the export panel to download the palette in CSS, Tailwind, SCSS, JSON, PNG, or SVG format.

Tip: start with complementary harmony for high-energy designs (e.g., call-to-action buttons) and analogous harmony for calming, editorial layouts.

What Is the Image Color Extractor?

The Image Color Extractor is a free online tool that analyzes any uploaded photograph and extracts its dominant colors into a cohesive five-color palette. It uses advanced color-quantization algorithms to identify the most visually significant hues in an image, giving designers and creatives a data-driven starting point for their projects.

Photography is one of the richest sources of color inspiration. A sunset landscape, a street-food market, a fashion editorial, or a vintage film still all contain palettes that have been refined by nature, culture, or a photographer's eye. Extracting those palettes manually is tedious — this tool automates the process in seconds.

Common use cases include building brand palettes inspired by mood-board photography, creating social-media designs that harmonize with product shots, developing game-art color scripts from concept paintings, and generating data-visualization schemes from thematic imagery.

  • Drag-and-drop or click-to-upload interface
  • Supports JPEG, PNG, WebP, and GIF formats
  • Extracts five dominant colors with HEX values
  • Re-extract to get alternative color groupings
toolImage.howToContent:
How to Use the Image Color Extractor

Turn any photograph into a usable color palette in just a few steps.

  1. Upload an image — Drag and drop a photo onto the dropzone, or click to browse your files. The tool accepts JPEG, PNG, WebP, and GIF formats.
  2. Wait for extraction — The algorithm analyzes color distribution across the image. A brief loading indicator appears while processing.
  3. View the palette — Five dominant colors are displayed as swatches with their HEX codes. These represent the most visually prominent hues in your image.
  4. Re-extract — Click the Re-extract Colors button to run the algorithm again with different clustering parameters, producing an alternative palette from the same image.
  5. Copy colors — Click any swatch or HEX code to copy it to your clipboard for use in your design software or code editor.
  6. Export the palette — Use the export feature to download the palette as CSS variables, Tailwind config, SCSS, JSON, PNG, or SVG.

Tip: for the best results, use high-quality images with clear areas of distinct color. Busy, noisy photos may yield muddier palette results — try cropping to the most interesting area first.

toolContrast.aboutContent:
What Is the Contrast Checker?

The Contrast Checker is a free online accessibility tool that measures the color contrast ratio between any foreground (text) and background color pair. It then evaluates the result against the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 at both AA and AAA levels for normal and large text.

Accessibility is not optional — it is a legal and ethical requirement in many jurisdictions. Roughly 15% of the world's population lives with some form of disability, and poor color contrast is one of the most common barriers to reading digital content. Designers, developers, content creators, and QA testers use contrast checkers daily to validate that interfaces are usable by everyone.

Beyond compliance, good contrast improves readability for all users, especially in challenging environments such as bright sunlight on a mobile screen or low-quality projectors in a meeting room.

  • Tests against WCAG 2.1 AA and AAA criteria
  • Evaluates both normal text (min 4.5:1) and large text (min 3:1)
  • Instant visual preview with sample text
  • Swap foreground and background colors in one click
toolContrast.howToContent:
How to Use the Contrast Checker

Verifying that your color choices meet accessibility standards takes just a few seconds with this tool.

  1. Set the foreground color — Click the Foreground (Text) color picker or paste a HEX code to choose your text color.
  2. Set the background color — Click the Background color picker or paste a HEX code to choose the surface behind your text.
  3. Read the contrast ratio — The tool instantly calculates and displays the contrast ratio (e.g., 7.4:1).
  4. Check WCAG results — Four compliance badges show Pass or Fail for AA Normal, AA Large, AAA Normal, and AAA Large text.
  5. Preview sample text — A live preview renders large and small text using your chosen colors so you can judge readability at a glance.
  6. Swap colors — Click the Swap button to reverse foreground and background and check the inverse combination.
  7. Adjust until passing — If a combination fails, slightly lighten or darken one of the colors and watch the ratio update in real time until you reach the desired WCAG level.

Pro tip: aim for AAA compliance (7:1) wherever possible — it provides the best experience for users with low vision or color deficiencies.

understanding-color-theory-basics.title: Understanding Color Theory Basics: A Complete Guide for Designers
understanding-color-theory-basics.excerpt: Master the fundamentals of color theory, from the color wheel to primary, secondary, and tertiary colors. Learn how colors interact and create visual harmony.
understanding-color-theory-basics.content:
What is Color Theory?

Color theory is the science and art of using color. It explains how humans perceive color and provides guidance for creating effective color combinations. Understanding color theory is essential for any designer, artist, or creative professional working with visual media.

The Color Wheel

The color wheel is the fundamental tool of color theory. First developed by Sir Isaac Newton in 1666, it organizes colors in a circle to show relationships between primary, secondary, and tertiary colors.

Primary Colors

Primary colors are the foundation of all other colors. In traditional color theory (used in painting), the primary colors are red, yellow, and blue. These colors cannot be created by mixing other colors together.

Secondary Colors

Secondary colors are created by mixing two primary colors:

  • Orange = Red + Yellow
  • Green = Yellow + Blue
  • Purple = Blue + Red

Tertiary Colors

Tertiary colors result from mixing a primary color with an adjacent secondary color. Examples include red-orange, yellow-green, and blue-violet. These colors add nuance and depth to your palette.

Color Properties

Every color has three main properties that define its appearance:

Hue

Hue is the pure color itself—what we commonly call 'color.' Red, blue, green, and yellow are all different hues. Hue is determined by the wavelength of light.

Saturation (Chroma)

Saturation refers to the intensity or purity of a color. A highly saturated color is vivid and bright, while a desaturated color appears muted or grayish. Reducing saturation creates softer, more subtle tones.

Value (Brightness)

Value describes how light or dark a color is. Adding white to a color creates a tint (lighter value), while adding black creates a shade (darker value). Value is crucial for creating contrast and visual hierarchy.

Understanding Color Relationships

Colors don't exist in isolation—they interact with each other. Understanding these relationships helps you create harmonious and effective color schemes.

Warm vs Cool Colors

Colors are often categorized as warm or cool:

  • Warm colors (red, orange, yellow) are energetic and advance visually
  • Cool colors (blue, green, purple) are calming and recede visually

Using warm and cool colors strategically can create depth, mood, and emphasis in your designs.

Complementary Colors

Complementary colors sit opposite each other on the color wheel (like red and green, or blue and orange). When placed together, they create maximum contrast and vibration, making each color appear more intense.

Practical Applications

Understanding color theory helps you make informed design decisions. Use the color wheel to create balanced palettes, leverage contrast for emphasis, and understand how colors will interact before implementing them in your projects.

Tools for Color Theory

Digital tools like Kolr make it easy to apply color theory principles. Our color harmony explorer helps you generate complementary, analogous, and triadic schemes automatically, while our contrast checker ensures your color choices meet accessibility standards.

By mastering these color theory basics, you'll have a strong foundation for creating beautiful, effective color palettes for any design project.

creating-accessible-color-palettes.title: Creating Accessible Color Palettes: WCAG Guidelines and Best Practices
creating-accessible-color-palettes.excerpt: Learn how to design color palettes that everyone can use. Comprehensive guide to WCAG contrast ratios, color blindness considerations, and accessibility testing.
creating-accessible-color-palettes.content:
Why Color Accessibility Matters

Approximately 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women have some form of color vision deficiency. Additionally, users with low vision, older adults, and people using devices in bright sunlight all benefit from accessible color choices. Creating accessible color palettes isn't just about compliance—it's about inclusive design that works for everyone.

Understanding WCAG Contrast Standards

The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) provide specific contrast ratio requirements for text and interactive elements.

WCAG AA Standards (Minimum)

  • Normal text: Minimum contrast ratio of 4.5:1
  • Large text (18pt+ or 14pt+ bold): Minimum contrast ratio of 3:1
  • UI components: Minimum contrast ratio of 3:1 for interface elements

WCAG AAA Standards (Enhanced)

  • Normal text: Minimum contrast ratio of 7:1
  • Large text: Minimum contrast ratio of 4.5:1

Meeting AAA standards provides the best readability and is recommended for text-heavy applications, educational content, and interfaces used by older adults.

Choosing Accessible Color Combinations

High Contrast is Key

The most reliable way to ensure accessibility is to use high contrast between text and backgrounds. Dark text on light backgrounds or light text on dark backgrounds typically work best.

Don't Rely on Color Alone

Never use color as the only way to convey information. Always pair color with text labels, icons, patterns, or other visual indicators. For example, don't just show errors in red—also include an error icon and descriptive text.

Test with Actual Tools

Use tools like Kolr's contrast checker to verify your color combinations meet WCAG standards before implementing them. Testing early in the design process saves time and prevents accessibility issues.

Color Blindness Considerations

Different types of color vision deficiency affect how people perceive colors:

  • Protanopia/Deuteranopia (red-green color blindness): Difficulty distinguishing reds and greens
  • Tritanopia (blue-yellow color blindness): Difficulty distinguishing blues and yellows
  • Achromatopsia (total color blindness): Rare condition where no colors are perceived

Safe Color Combinations

Some color combinations work well for most types of color blindness:

  • Blue and orange
  • Blue and yellow (but ensure sufficient contrast)
  • Dark colors with white or light backgrounds
  • Avoid red-green combinations without additional indicators

Practical Tips for Accessible Palettes

1. Start with Grayscale

Design your interface in grayscale first to ensure your information hierarchy works without color. Then add color to enhance, not replace, the existing clarity.

2. Use Sufficient Color Contrast

Aim for at least 4.5:1 contrast for body text. For critical elements like call-to-action buttons, aim even higher.

3. Provide Multiple Visual Cues

Combine color with shape, position, text labels, and icons to convey meaning.

4. Test Your Designs

Use color blindness simulators and contrast checkers throughout your design process. Get feedback from users with different types of color vision.

5. Document Your Decisions

Create a style guide that documents which color combinations meet accessibility standards and how they should be used in your product.

Tools and Resources

Kolr's contrast checker makes it easy to verify WCAG compliance in real-time. Simply input your foreground and background colors to see if they meet AA and AAA standards for different text sizes.

By prioritizing accessibility in your color palette choices, you create designs that are beautiful, functional, and inclusive for all users.

color-psychology-in-design.content:
The Power of Color Psychology

Colors do more than make designs look attractive—they trigger emotional responses, influence perceptions, and even affect behavior. Understanding color psychology helps you make strategic color choices that support your design objectives and connect with your audience on a deeper level.

Common Color Associations

Red: Energy, Passion, Urgency

Red is the most stimulating color. It increases heart rate and creates a sense of urgency. In design, red is effective for:

  • Call-to-action buttons (especially for sales and urgent actions)
  • Highlighting important information or warnings
  • Food and beverage brands (stimulates appetite)
  • Energetic and bold brand identities

Caution: Red can also signify danger or error. Use it thoughtfully to avoid creating unintended stress or anxiety.

Blue: Trust, Calm, Professionalism

Blue is the most universally liked color. It evokes feelings of trust, stability, and calm. Blue is ideal for:

  • Financial services and healthcare (builds trust)
  • Technology companies (suggests innovation and reliability)
  • Corporate and professional contexts
  • Creating calming, peaceful environments

Caution: Too much blue can feel cold or impersonal. Balance it with warmer accent colors.

Green: Growth, Nature, Health

Green represents nature, growth, and renewal. It's associated with health, sustainability, and prosperity. Use green for:

  • Environmental and sustainability brands
  • Health and wellness products
  • Financial growth and money-related contexts
  • Success indicators (like confirmation messages)

Yellow: Optimism, Happiness, Energy

Yellow is the brightest color and captures attention quickly. It conveys optimism, creativity, and warmth. Yellow works well for:

  • Highlighting important information
  • Creative and playful brands
  • Calls-to-action in moderation
  • Children's products

Caution: Pure bright yellow can be difficult to read and overwhelming in large doses. Use it as an accent color.

Orange: Enthusiasm, Creativity, Affordability

Orange combines red's energy with yellow's happiness. It's friendly, cheerful, and inviting. Orange is effective for:

  • Call-to-action buttons (less aggressive than red)
  • Budget-friendly brands
  • Creative and artistic contexts
  • Expressing enthusiasm and excitement

Purple: Luxury, Creativity, Spirituality

Purple has historically been associated with royalty and luxury. It also suggests creativity and imagination. Use purple for:

  • Premium and luxury products
  • Beauty and cosmetics
  • Creative and artistic brands
  • Spiritual or mystical themes

Black: Sophistication, Power, Elegance

Black conveys sophistication, luxury, and authority. It's timeless and creates strong contrast. Black works well for:

  • High-end and luxury brands
  • Creating visual hierarchy and emphasis
  • Modern, minimalist designs
  • Professional and formal contexts

White: Purity, Simplicity, Cleanliness

White represents purity, cleanliness, and simplicity. It's essential for creating breathing room in designs. Use white for:

  • Healthcare and medical contexts
  • Minimalist and modern designs
  • Creating contrast and emphasis
  • Technology and innovation brands

Cultural Considerations

Color meanings vary significantly across cultures. For example:

  • White symbolizes purity in Western cultures but mourning in some Eastern cultures
  • Red means luck and prosperity in China but can signify danger in Western contexts
  • Yellow represents courage in Japan but can mean cowardice in some Western contexts

Always research your target audience's cultural context when choosing colors for international products.

Combining Colors for Emotional Impact

Single colors create specific emotions, but color combinations amplify or modify these effects:

  • Blue + Orange: Professional yet friendly
  • Black + Gold: Luxury and elegance
  • Green + Brown: Natural and organic
  • Purple + Pink: Creative and playful

Practical Application

When choosing colors for your project:

  1. Define your goals: What emotions do you want to evoke?
  2. Know your audience: What colors resonate with them?
  3. Consider context: Where and how will users experience your design?
  4. Test and iterate: Use A/B testing to validate your color choices

Beyond Trends

While color trends come and go, color psychology remains constant. Focus on choosing colors that authentically represent your brand and resonate with your audience, rather than simply following the latest design trends.

By understanding color psychology, you can create designs that not only look beautiful but also effectively communicate your message and connect with your audience on an emotional level.

mastering-color-harmonies.title: Mastering Color Harmonies: From Complementary to Tetradic Schemes
mastering-color-harmonies.excerpt: Complete guide to color harmony rules. Learn when and how to use complementary, analogous, triadic, and tetradic color schemes for stunning designs.
mastering-color-harmonies.content:
What Are Color Harmonies?

Color harmonies are combinations of colors that are aesthetically pleasing and create visual balance. Based on the color wheel, these tried-and-true formulas help designers create cohesive palettes that work well together. Understanding color harmonies takes the guesswork out of color selection.

Monochromatic Harmony

What It Is

Monochromatic color schemes use variations of a single hue by changing its saturation and brightness. This creates palettes with different tints, shades, and tones of one color.

When to Use It

  • Creating sophisticated, cohesive designs
  • Emphasizing content over color
  • Minimalist and elegant aesthetics
  • When you need a safe, professional palette

Pros and Cons

Pros: Easy to create, always harmonious, sophisticated look
Cons: Can lack visual interest, may feel monotonous

Tips

  • Ensure sufficient contrast between values for readability
  • Use texture and typography to add visual interest
  • Consider adding a neutral (black, white, gray) for depth

Analogous Harmony

What It Is

Analogous schemes use colors that sit next to each other on the color wheel, typically three colors (like blue, blue-green, and green).

When to Use It

  • Creating natural, harmonious designs
  • Nature-inspired palettes
  • Designs that need to feel cohesive and calm
  • Gradients and backgrounds

Pros and Cons

Pros: Naturally harmonious, rich and nuanced, easy on the eyes
Cons: Low contrast, needs careful hierarchy

Tips

  • Choose one color as dominant
  • Use the other colors as accents
  • Add a neutral or complementary accent for emphasis

Complementary Harmony

What It Is

Complementary schemes use colors opposite each other on the color wheel (like blue and orange, or red and green).

When to Use It

  • Creating high contrast and visual impact
  • Making elements stand out
  • Energetic, bold designs
  • Call-to-action elements

Pros and Cons

Pros: Maximum contrast, vibrant and eye-catching, creates depth
Cons: Can be overwhelming if overused, challenging to balance

Tips

  • Use one color as dominant and the other as accent
  • Desaturate one or both colors for subtlety
  • Avoid using pure complementary colors in equal amounts
  • Use tints and shades to create variations

Split-Complementary Harmony

What It Is

Split-complementary uses a base color plus the two colors adjacent to its complement. For example, blue with yellow-orange and red-orange (instead of pure orange).

When to Use It

  • More nuanced than complementary
  • When you need contrast without intensity
  • Balanced, interesting palettes

Pros and Cons

Pros: Good contrast with more options, easier to balance than complementary
Cons: More complex to manage

Triadic Harmony

What It Is

Triadic schemes use three colors equally spaced around the color wheel (like red, yellow, and blue—the primary colors—or orange, green, and purple).

When to Use It

  • Vibrant, balanced designs
  • Playful and dynamic aesthetics
  • When you need variety with harmony
  • Children's products and creative projects

Pros and Cons

Pros: Vibrant, balanced, versatile
Cons: Can be overwhelming, requires careful balance

Tips

  • Let one color dominate
  • Use the other two as accents
  • Consider using tints and shades to soften intensity

Tetradic (Double-Complementary) Harmony

What It Is

Tetradic schemes use four colors arranged into two complementary pairs. This forms a rectangle or square on the color wheel.

When to Use It

  • Rich, complex palettes
  • When you need many color options
  • Experienced designers comfortable with complexity

Pros and Cons

Pros: Most variety, rich and complex, many options
Cons: Hardest to balance, can easily become chaotic

Tips

  • Choose one dominant color
  • Balance warm and cool colors
  • Use neutrals to give the eye rest
  • Test extensively before finalizing

Choosing the Right Harmony

Consider these factors when selecting a color harmony:

  • Brand identity: Does it match your brand personality?
  • Project goals: What emotion or action do you want to inspire?
  • Audience: What will resonate with your users?
  • Context: Where will the design be used?
  • Complexity: How much visual interest do you need?

Tools for Creating Harmonies

Kolr's color harmony explorer automatically generates harmonious palettes based on these principles. Simply choose a base color and select your desired harmony type to instantly see complementary, analogous, triadic, and other schemes.

By mastering these color harmonies, you'll have a systematic approach to creating beautiful, balanced color palettes for any design project.

extracting-colors-from-photos.title: Extracting Colors from Photos: Techniques and Best Practices
extracting-colors-from-photos.excerpt: Learn how to extract perfect color palettes from photographs. Tips for choosing source images, analyzing dominant colors, and creating usable design palettes.
extracting-colors-from-photos.content:
Why Extract Colors from Photos?

Photographs contain naturally harmonious color combinations created by nature, lighting, and real-world contexts. Extracting colors from photos is an excellent way to create authentic, balanced palettes for your design projects. Whether you're designing a website, creating a brand identity, or working on illustration, photo-based palettes provide instant inspiration and proven color harmony.

Choosing the Right Source Image

Look for Images with Clear Color Stories

The best source images have a clear color narrative. Look for photos with:

  • 3-5 distinct, well-represented colors
  • Good lighting (not overexposed or too dark)
  • Intentional composition
  • Colors that reflect the mood you want to convey

Consider Your Project Context

Match your source image to your project goals:

  • Nature photos: Organic, calming palettes
  • Urban scenes: Modern, edgy combinations
  • Food photography: Appetizing, warm tones
  • Fashion: Trendy, curated color stories
  • Art and interiors: Sophisticated, intentional palettes

Avoid Common Pitfalls

  • Too many colors: Busy images create muddled palettes
  • Poor lighting: Results in muddy, inaccurate colors
  • Heavy filters: Can create unrealistic color relationships
  • Low resolution: May not provide accurate color data

Understanding Dominant vs. Accent Colors

Dominant Colors

These are the colors that appear most frequently in the image. They typically form the background or main elements. In your design, dominant colors should be used for:

  • Backgrounds
  • Large sections or containers
  • Primary UI elements

Accent Colors

Accent colors appear less frequently but catch the eye—like a red flower in a green field. Use accent colors for:

  • Call-to-action buttons
  • Important highlights
  • Interactive elements
  • Creating visual interest

Extraction Techniques

Automatic Extraction

Tools like Kolr use sophisticated algorithms to identify the most significant colors in an image. These tools analyze:

  • Color frequency
  • Spatial distribution
  • Perceptual importance
  • Color clustering

Manual Selection

Sometimes you'll want to manually pick specific colors from an image rather than using automatic extraction. This works well when:

  • You want to emphasize a particular element
  • The automatic extraction misses a key color
  • You're building a palette around one hero color

Refining Your Extracted Palette

Adjust for Digital Use

Colors in photos may need adjustment for screen use:

  • Brighten dark colors: Photos often contain very dark values that don't work well as UI colors
  • Increase saturation: Photos can be slightly desaturated; boost saturation for more vibrant UI elements
  • Adjust for contrast: Ensure your palette has sufficient contrast for accessibility

Create Color Variations

Extend your extracted palette by creating:

  • Tints: Add white to create lighter versions (for backgrounds, hover states)
  • Shades: Add black to create darker versions (for text, depth)
  • Tones: Add gray to create muted versions (for disabled states, secondary elements)

Test in Context

Always test your extracted palette in your actual design:

  • Apply colors to real UI components
  • Check readability and contrast
  • Verify the mood matches your goals
  • Get feedback from others

Common Use Cases

Brand Identity

Extract colors from photos that represent your brand values—nature photos for eco-brands, city scenes for urban products, etc.

Web Design

Use photo extraction to create cohesive color schemes that match header images or hero photography on your site.

Presentation Design

Extract colors from presentation images to create matching slide backgrounds, text colors, and accent elements.

Product Design

Draw inspiration from product photography or lifestyle images to create UI themes that feel authentic and connected to the physical product.

Using Kolr for Photo Extraction

Kolr makes photo extraction effortless:

  1. Upload your image or use your device camera
  2. Automatic analysis identifies the 5 most important colors
  3. Copy hex codes with one tap for use in your design tools
  4. Save to your gallery for future reference

You can also use Kolr's web-based image extractor tool to experiment with different photos and immediately see the resulting palettes.

Best Practices Summary

  • Choose images with clear, intentional color stories
  • Look for photos with good lighting and 3-5 distinct colors
  • Understand the difference between dominant and accent colors
  • Adjust extracted colors for digital use and accessibility
  • Create variations (tints, shades, tones) for a complete palette
  • Always test your palette in the actual design context

By mastering the art of color extraction from photos, you'll never run out of palette inspiration. Real-world imagery provides endless combinations that are naturally balanced and visually appealing.

color-trends-2026.title: Color Trends 2026: The Palettes Shaping Design This Year
color-trends-2026.excerpt: Explore the dominant color trends of 2026, from digital lavender to earth-toned minimalism. Stay ahead with palettes that define modern design.
color-trends-2026.content:
The Color Landscape of 2026

Every year brings new color trends that influence everything from fashion and interior design to digital interfaces and branding. 2026 is defined by a tension between technological futurism and organic warmth—designers are blending digital aesthetics with natural tones to create palettes that feel both innovative and grounded.

Digital Lavender Continues to Dominate

Digital Lavender (#E6E0F3) has evolved from a trend color to a design staple. Its calming, gender-neutral quality makes it perfect for wellness apps, tech brands seeking approachability, and any design that needs to feel serene yet modern.

How to Use It

  • Pair with deep navy or charcoal for contrast
  • Use as a background for content-heavy interfaces
  • Combine with soft mint for a fresh, airy palette

Warm Earth Tones

Terracotta (#CC6B49), warm sand (#E8D5B7), and clay (#B87A5E) are everywhere in 2026. These colors connect digital experiences to the physical world, creating a sense of authenticity and groundedness.

Applications

  • E-commerce and lifestyle brands
  • Interior design and architecture portfolios
  • Sustainable and eco-conscious branding

Electric Teal

A vibrant teal (#00BFA6) is the accent color of the year. It provides energy without the aggressiveness of pure cyan, making it ideal for CTAs, highlights, and interactive elements.

Monochromatic Grays with Color Pops

Designers are embracing sophisticated gray palettes (#F5F5F5, #9E9E9E, #424242) punctuated by single bold accent colors. This approach creates clean, professional designs with strategic focal points.

Neo-Pastels

Unlike traditional pastels, neo-pastels have more saturation and depth. Think dusty rose (#D4A5A5), muted coral (#E07A5F), and sage (#87A878). They bring softness without looking washed out.

Dark Mode Refinement

Dark mode palettes are becoming more nuanced. Instead of pure black backgrounds, designers are using warm dark tones (#1A1A2E, #16213E) with carefully chosen accent colors that maintain readability and reduce eye strain.

How to Apply These Trends

For Brand Design

Choose one or two trend colors that align with your brand values. Don't chase every trend—authenticity matters more than novelty.

For UI Design

Incorporate trend colors as accent elements while maintaining a solid, accessible base palette. Ensure all color choices meet WCAG contrast requirements.

For Personal Projects

Trends are a great starting point for exploration. Use them as inspiration, then customize to create something uniquely yours.

building-brand-color-systems.title: Building Brand Color Systems: From Primary to Extended Palettes
building-brand-color-systems.excerpt: Learn how to create comprehensive brand color systems that scale. From choosing primary colors to building systematic color hierarchies.
building-brand-color-systems.content:
What Is a Brand Color System?

A brand color system goes beyond picking a few colors you like. It's a structured, hierarchical collection of colors designed to work together across every touchpoint—from your website and app to print materials and social media.

The Color Hierarchy

Primary Colors (1-2 colors)

These are your brand's signature colors. They appear in your logo, key CTAs, and major brand elements. Choose colors that reflect your brand personality and differentiate you from competitors.

Secondary Colors (2-3 colors)

Secondary colors support and complement the primary palette. They provide variety without competing for attention. Use them for supporting UI elements, section backgrounds, and visual accents.

Neutral Colors (3-5 shades)

Neutrals are the workhorses of your color system. They handle text, backgrounds, borders, and spacers. Create a range from near-white to near-black with consistent warmth or coolness.

Semantic Colors

These communicate system states: success (green), warning (amber), error (red), and info (blue). Even if they don't match your brand palette, they must be consistent and accessible.

Building Your System Step by Step

Step 1: Define Your Brand Attributes

Before choosing colors, define what your brand stands for. Is it energetic or calm? Premium or accessible? Technical or creative? These attributes guide your color choices.

Step 2: Choose Your Primary Color

Start with one hero color that embodies your brand. Test it in context—on buttons, headers, and links. Ensure it works on both light and dark backgrounds.

Step 3: Generate a Scale

For each color in your system, create a scale of 9-11 shades from lightest to darkest. This ensures you have the right shade for every use case:

  • 50-100: Subtle backgrounds
  • 200-300: Borders and dividers
  • 400-500: Icons and secondary text
  • 600-700: Primary elements and links
  • 800-900: Text and high-emphasis elements

Step 4: Test for Accessibility

Every color combination in your system should meet WCAG AA standards at minimum. Test text colors against backgrounds, and ensure interactive elements have sufficient contrast.

Step 5: Document Everything

Create a style guide that specifies when and how to use each color. Include hex values, RGB values, and usage examples.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Too many primary colors: Dilutes brand recognition
  • Ignoring accessibility: Beautiful colors that fail contrast tests are useless
  • No neutral palette: Forces you to use brand colors where neutrals work better
  • Inconsistent naming: Use a clear naming convention (brand-primary-600, not "dark blue")

Tools for Building Color Systems

Use Kolr's color harmony explorer to find complementary and analogous colors for your primary palette. The contrast checker verifies accessibility, and the export feature outputs your system in CSS variables, Tailwind config, or JSON tokens—ready for implementation.

digital-color-spaces-explained.title: Digital Color Spaces Explained: sRGB, Display P3, and Lab
digital-color-spaces-explained.excerpt: Understand the differences between sRGB, Display P3, and Lab color spaces. Learn which to use for web, print, and modern HDR displays.
digital-color-spaces-explained.content:
Why Color Spaces Matter

Have you ever created a design on your screen that looked completely different when printed or viewed on another device? Color spaces are the reason. A color space defines the range (gamut) of colors that can be represented in a system. Understanding color spaces helps you ensure your colors look consistent everywhere.

sRGB: The Web Standard

What It Is

sRGB (standard Red Green Blue) was created in 1996 by HP and Microsoft. It's the default color space for the web, and most monitors and devices display sRGB.

Gamut

sRGB covers about 35% of the visible color spectrum. While this sounds limited, it's been sufficient for most digital content for decades.

When to Use It

  • Web design and development (CSS colors are sRGB by default)
  • Email design
  • Social media graphics
  • Any content viewed primarily on standard monitors

Display P3: The Modern Standard

What It Is

Display P3 was developed by Apple and is based on the DCI-P3 color space used in digital cinema. It offers about 25% more colors than sRGB, especially in reds, greens, and oranges.

Support

All recent Apple devices, many Android phones, and newer monitors support Display P3. CSS now supports P3 colors via the color(display-p3 r g b) function.

When to Use It

  • Designs targeting modern devices
  • Photography and image-heavy content
  • Brands using vibrant reds, greens, or oranges that look muted in sRGB
  • HDR content

Lab (CIELAB): Perceptually Uniform

What It Is

Lab is a color space designed to be perceptually uniform—meaning a numerical change in value corresponds to a similar perceived change in color. It separates lightness (L) from color information (a = green-red, b = blue-yellow).

Advantages

  • Device-independent: represents colors as humans perceive them
  • Great for generating consistent color scales
  • Used by CSS lab() and oklch() functions

When to Use It

  • Creating perceptually even color gradients
  • Building design token systems
  • Color analysis and comparison

OKLCH: The Future of CSS Color

OKLCH (Oklab Lightness Chroma Hue) is gaining traction as the most intuitive color space for designers. It uses familiar concepts—lightness, saturation (chroma), and hue angle—while maintaining perceptual uniformity.

CSS Syntax

Use oklch(70% 0.15 240) in CSS to define colors with predictable lightness and vivid control over hue.

Practical Recommendations

  • For web: Use sRGB hex/rgb() as your base, with P3 as progressive enhancement
  • For design systems: Define colors in OKLCH or Lab for perceptual consistency, then convert to sRGB/P3 for implementation
  • For print: Work in CMYK, but understand your source colors in Lab for accurate conversion

Testing Across Color Spaces

Always preview your designs on multiple devices. A color that looks vibrant in P3 may appear flat in sRGB. Kolr helps you work in standard hex (sRGB) with tools to ensure your colors are accessible and harmonious across devices.

color-in-ui-design.title: Color in UI/UX Design: Principles for Better Interfaces
color-in-ui-design.excerpt: Master the use of color in user interfaces. Learn about color hierarchy, interactive states, feedback colors, and creating intuitive experiences.
color-in-ui-design.content:
The Role of Color in UI Design

Color in UI design serves a functional purpose beyond aesthetics. It guides users, communicates status, creates hierarchy, and influences behavior. A well-designed color system makes interfaces intuitive, while poor color choices create confusion and frustration.

Establishing Visual Hierarchy

Primary Actions

Use your strongest brand color for primary CTAs—the buttons and links users should notice first. High saturation and contrast ensure these elements stand out.

Secondary Actions

Secondary buttons and links should be visually subordinate. Use outlined buttons, lower-contrast colors, or neutrals to differentiate them from primary actions.

Tertiary/Ghost Actions

Text links and ghost buttons should be the least visually prominent. Use your brand color at lower opacity or rely on text styling (underlines) instead of color alone.

Interactive States

Every interactive element needs multiple color states:

  • Default: The base appearance
  • Hover: Slightly brighter/darker to confirm interactivity
  • Active/Pressed: More pronounced change to confirm the click
  • Focus: Visible outline for keyboard navigation (critical for accessibility)
  • Disabled: Desaturated and low-contrast to indicate non-interactivity

System Feedback Colors

Success (Green)

Use green for confirmations, completed actions, and positive status. Avoid using green only—add icons and text labels.

Warning (Amber/Yellow)

Warnings indicate potential issues that don't block the user. Use warm tones that attract attention without alarm.

Error (Red)

Errors demand immediate attention. Use red sparingly and always pair with descriptive messages explaining what went wrong and how to fix it.

Information (Blue)

Blue conveys neutral information—tips, updates, and non-critical messages.

Color and Typography

Body text should use near-black or dark gray (#1A1A1A to #333333) on light backgrounds, or near-white (#E0E0E0 to #FFFFFF) on dark backgrounds. Never use pure black on pure white—it creates harsh contrast that strains eyes.

Link Colors

Links need to be distinguishable from body text. Use your brand color and ensure a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 against surrounding text.

Dark Mode Considerations

Don't simply invert your light mode colors. Dark mode requires:

  • Desaturated primary colors (vivid colors on dark backgrounds cause visual vibration)
  • Elevated surfaces using lighter shades of your dark background (not just opacity)
  • Adjusted shadows (use darker shadows or remove them entirely)

Testing Your UI Colors

Use Kolr's contrast checker to verify all text-background combinations meet WCAG standards. Test on multiple devices, in both light and dark environments, and with colorblind simulation to ensure your interface works for everyone.

gradient-design-techniques.title: Gradient Design Techniques: From Subtle to Bold
gradient-design-techniques.excerpt: Master the art of CSS gradients. Learn linear, radial, and conic techniques, avoid muddy midpoints, and create gradients that enhance your designs.
gradient-design-techniques.content:
The Renaissance of Gradients

After years of flat design dominance, gradients have made a powerful comeback. Modern gradients are more refined—used strategically to add depth, energy, and visual interest without overwhelming the design.

Types of CSS Gradients

Linear Gradients

The most common type, linear gradients transition colors along a straight line. The angle controls the direction:

  • linear-gradient(to right, #FF0000, #0000FF) — horizontal
  • linear-gradient(180deg, #FF0000, #0000FF) — top to bottom
  • linear-gradient(45deg, #FF0000, #0000FF) — diagonal

Radial Gradients

Radial gradients emanate from a center point outward. They're perfect for spotlight effects, circular elements, and background focal points.

Conic Gradients

Conic gradients rotate colors around a center point, like a color wheel. They're excellent for pie charts, loading indicators, and decorative elements.

Avoiding Muddy Midpoints

The biggest gradient mistake is choosing colors that create a muddy gray or brown in the middle. This happens when complementary colors mix through the center of the color space.

Solutions

  • Add a midpoint color: Insert a third color between your start and end to control the transition
  • Use analogous colors: Colors next to each other on the wheel always blend beautifully
  • Control color stops: Adjust the position of each color to minimize the muddy zone
  • Use OKLCH interpolation: CSS now supports in oklch for perceptually smooth gradients

Gradient Best Practices

Subtle Backgrounds

For backgrounds, use low-opacity gradients or similar hues. A gradient from #FAFAFA to #F0F0F0 adds dimension without distraction.

Bold Hero Sections

Hero gradients can be dramatic. Use high-saturation colors with enough contrast for overlaid text. Always test text readability across the entire gradient.

Glassmorphism

Combine subtle gradients with backdrop-blur for modern glass effects. Use semi-transparent colors (rgba) for the gradient base.

Multi-Color Gradients

Three or more colors create rich, complex gradients. Tips:

  • Distribute color stops evenly or cluster them for intentional transitions
  • Use colors from the same temperature family (all warm or all cool)
  • Preview at actual display size—gradients look different at different scales

Performance Considerations

CSS gradients are rendered by the browser and have minimal performance impact. They're almost always better than gradient images because they scale perfectly and load instantly.

Try It Now

Use Kolr's gradient generator to experiment with linear, radial, and conic gradients. Pick colors, adjust angles, and copy the CSS code directly into your project.

color-accessibility-beyond-contrast.title: Beyond Contrast: Advanced Color Accessibility Techniques
color-accessibility-beyond-contrast.excerpt: Go beyond basic contrast ratios. Learn about color blindness design patterns, APCA, non-color indicators, and inclusive design practices.
color-accessibility-beyond-contrast.content:
Accessibility Is More Than Contrast

While contrast ratios are the most well-known aspect of color accessibility, true inclusive design goes much further. This guide covers advanced techniques for making your color choices work for everyone.

Understanding APCA

The Accessible Perceptual Contrast Algorithm (APCA) is the next generation of contrast measurement, planned for WCAG 3.0. Unlike the current WCAG 2.x formula, APCA accounts for:

  • Polarity sensitivity (dark text on light vs. light text on dark)
  • Font size and weight
  • Spatial frequency (text vs. non-text elements)

Key Differences

Under APCA, light text on dark backgrounds needs higher contrast than dark text on light backgrounds—matching how human vision actually works. This means your dark mode designs may need adjustments you wouldn't catch with WCAG 2.x testing alone.

Designing for Color Blindness

Common Patterns

About 8% of men and 0.5% of women have some form of color vision deficiency. The most common types confuse reds and greens (protanopia and deuteranopia).

Design Strategies

  • Never rely on color alone: Always pair color with shape, pattern, text, or icons
  • Use blue as your safe accent: Blue is distinguishable by all common types of color blindness
  • Add textures to charts: Use patterns (stripes, dots, crosshatch) in addition to colors for data visualization
  • Provide color-coded alternatives: Let users customize or choose from colorblind-friendly palettes

Non-Color Indicators

Ensure every piece of information conveyed by color is also conveyed by something else:

  • Form validation: Red border + error icon + error text
  • Status badges: Color + text label ("Active", "Pending")
  • Links: Color + underline (or other text decoration)
  • Charts: Color + pattern + labels

Focus Indicators

Keyboard users rely on focus indicators to navigate. Default browser outlines are functional but often overridden by designers. If you customize focus styles:

  • Ensure the focus indicator has at least 3:1 contrast against the background
  • Make it at least 2px thick
  • Consider using both outline and background change for maximum visibility

Motion and Color

Some users are sensitive to motion, and rapidly changing colors can trigger seizures or migraines. Follow these guidelines:

  • Avoid flashing content (more than 3 flashes per second)
  • Respect prefers-reduced-motion media query
  • Make color transitions smooth and optional

Testing Comprehensively

Use Kolr's colorblind simulator to test your palette across protanopia, deuteranopia, tritanopia, and achromatopsia. Combine this with contrast checking to ensure your design is truly accessible.

monochromatic-design-guide.title: The Power of Monochromatic Design: Less Color, More Impact
monochromatic-design-guide.excerpt: Discover why monochromatic palettes create some of the most elegant designs. Learn techniques for building depth with a single hue.
monochromatic-design-guide.content:
Why Monochromatic?

Monochromatic design uses variations of a single color—different tints, shades, and tones—to create an entire visual experience. Far from being boring, monochromatic palettes create some of the most sophisticated and cohesive designs in the world.

The Psychology of Monochrome

Monochromatic designs feel intentional and refined. They communicate focus, consistency, and brand confidence. When you limit your palette to one hue, every other design element (typography, spacing, imagery) gets to shine.

Building a Monochromatic Scale

Start with Your Base Hue

Choose a color that represents your brand or project mood. Consider the emotional associations—blue for trust, green for growth, purple for creativity.

Create 9-11 Steps

Generate a scale from very light (near-white tint) to very dark (near-black shade):

  • 50: Barely tinted background
  • 100-200: Subtle backgrounds and borders
  • 300-400: Secondary elements
  • 500: Your base/primary shade
  • 600-700: Primary text and buttons
  • 800-900: Headings and high-emphasis elements
  • 950: Near-black for body text

Adding Depth Without New Colors

Use Value Contrast

The key to monochromatic success is strong value contrast. Pair your lightest shades with darkest shades for maximum readability.

Leverage Opacity

Use opacity variations to create subtle layering effects. Glass-like overlays at different opacities add dimension without introducing new hues.

Incorporate Texture

Subtle textures, gradients, and shadows within your single hue create rich visual experiences.

When to Use Monochromatic

  • Luxury and premium brands
  • Editorial and content-focused designs
  • Portfolios and galleries
  • Documentation and technical content
  • When you want content (images, video) to be the star

Common Pitfalls

  • Insufficient contrast: Adjacent shades may look different on your screen but identical on others
  • No focal point: Without a contrasting accent, users may not know where to look
  • Monotony in long content: Break up long pages with images or subtle gradients

The Accent Exception

Many "monochromatic" designs strategically use one accent color for CTAs and key interactions. This creates a powerful focal point while maintaining the elegance of a single-hue palette.

color-for-data-visualization.title: Color for Data Visualization: Making Charts Clear and Accessible
color-for-data-visualization.excerpt: Learn how to use color effectively in charts, graphs, and dashboards. Build palettes that are both beautiful and readable for all users.
color-for-data-visualization.content:
Why Data Visualization Color Matters

In data visualization, color isn't decorative—it's a data dimension. Poor color choices can mislead users, hide patterns, or make data impossible to read for colorblind users. Good color choices make complex data instantly understandable.

Types of Color Scales

Sequential Scales

Use a single hue progressing from light to dark to represent ordered data (low to high, less to more). Example: light blue to dark blue for temperature ranges.

Diverging Scales

Use two contrasting hues with a neutral midpoint for data that has a meaningful center (positive/negative, above/below average). Example: red through white to blue.

Categorical Scales

Use distinct, easily distinguishable colors for categories with no inherent order. This is the hardest type to get right for accessibility.

Building Accessible Data Palettes

Maximum 7 Categories

Research shows humans can reliably distinguish about 7 colors simultaneously. Beyond that, add patterns, labels, or interactive filtering.

Ensure Lightness Variation

Don't just vary hue—vary lightness too. This ensures categories remain distinguishable in grayscale and for colorblind users.

Avoid Red-Green Pairs

The most common color blindness affects red-green distinction. Use blue-orange or blue-red-yellow instead.

Practical Guidelines

  • Test in grayscale: If your chart is unreadable in grayscale, it fails for many users
  • Add labels directly: Label data series directly on the chart rather than relying on color-coded legends
  • Use colorblind-safe palettes: Pre-built palettes like ColorBrewer are designed for data visualization accessibility
  • Consider cultural associations: Red means loss in Western finance but luck in Chinese culture

Dashboard Color Strategy

For dashboards with multiple charts:

  • Use a consistent categorical palette across all charts
  • Reserve red and green for semantic meaning (alerts, success)
  • Keep backgrounds neutral to let data colors stand out
  • Use color sparingly—not every chart element needs a different color

Tools for Data Color

Use Kolr's color harmony tools to create balanced categorical palettes. Test them with the colorblind simulator to ensure all categories remain distinguishable, then export as JSON for direct integration with charting libraries.

seasonal-color-palettes.title: Seasonal Color Palettes for Design Projects
seasonal-color-palettes.excerpt: Create season-inspired palettes that evoke specific moods. From spring freshness to winter elegance, master the art of seasonal color design.
seasonal-color-palettes.content:
Why Seasonal Colors Work

Seasonal color palettes tap into deep psychological associations formed by our experience of the natural world. When you use colors that evoke a specific season, you create an immediate emotional connection with your audience—before they even read a word.

Spring Palettes

Characteristics

Light, fresh, and vibrant. Spring colors are about new beginnings, growth, and optimism.

Key Colors

  • Mint green (#98FB98)
  • Soft pink (#FFB7C5)
  • Butter yellow (#FFFACD)
  • Lavender (#E6E6FA)
  • Sky blue (#87CEEB)

Best For

Product launches, wellness brands, children's designs, fresh rebrandings, and spring marketing campaigns.

Summer Palettes

Characteristics

Bold, saturated, and energetic. Summer colors radiate warmth, fun, and adventure.

Key Colors

  • Coral (#FF6F61)
  • Ocean blue (#006994)
  • Sunshine yellow (#FFD700)
  • Tropical green (#00B16A)
  • Hot pink (#FF69B4)

Best For

Event promotions, travel brands, food and beverage, entertainment, and lifestyle content.

Autumn Palettes

Characteristics

Warm, rich, and grounded. Autumn colors feel sophisticated, cozy, and nostalgic.

Key Colors

  • Burnt orange (#CC5500)
  • Deep red (#8B0000)
  • Mustard (#FFDB58)
  • Olive green (#556B2F)
  • Chocolate brown (#7B3F00)

Best For

Fashion brands, coffee and food, publishing, artisanal products, and Thanksgiving campaigns.

Winter Palettes

Characteristics

Cool, crisp, and elegant. Winter colors can be icy and minimal or rich and festive.

Key Colors

  • Ice blue (#D6ECEF)
  • Silver (#C0C0C0)
  • Deep navy (#001F3F)
  • Cranberry (#9B1B30)
  • Evergreen (#2C5F2D)

Best For

Luxury brands, holiday campaigns, corporate events, winter sports, and year-end reviews.

Using Seasonal Palettes Strategically

Don't just follow the calendar. Use seasonal palettes when they align with your message. A cozy autumn palette can work year-round for a coffee brand, just as cool winter tones suit a premium tech brand in any month.

Build Your Own

Use Kolr's gallery for seasonal inspiration, then customize with the color harmony explorer to create a palette that's uniquely yours while capturing the essence of any season.

dark-mode-color-strategies.title: Dark Mode Color Strategies: Beyond Inverting Your Palette
dark-mode-color-strategies.excerpt: Design effective dark mode interfaces with proper color adaptation. Learn about surface elevation, desaturation, and maintaining brand consistency.
dark-mode-color-strategies.content:
Dark Mode Is Not Color Inversion

The biggest mistake designers make with dark mode is simply inverting their light mode colors. True dark mode requires a thoughtful approach to surface colors, contrast, brand expression, and readability.

Surface Elevation

The Layer System

In dark mode, elevation is communicated through lighter surface colors (not shadows, which are invisible on dark backgrounds):

  • Background: #121212 or similar very dark (not pure black)
  • Surface Level 1: #1E1E1E (cards, modals)
  • Surface Level 2: #252525 (elevated cards, popovers)
  • Surface Level 3: #2C2C2C (highest elevation)

Why Not Pure Black?

Pure black (#000000) creates excessive contrast with white text, causing visual fatigue. It also makes surfaces feel like "holes" in the interface. Use dark grays instead for a more comfortable experience.

Color Desaturation

Vivid colors on dark backgrounds create visual vibration—an uncomfortable optical effect where bright colors seem to buzz against dark surroundings. Solution: reduce saturation by 10-30% for dark mode.

Examples

  • Light mode blue: #2196F3 → Dark mode blue: #64B5F6
  • Light mode green: #4CAF50 → Dark mode green: #81C784
  • Light mode red: #F44336 → Dark mode red: #E57373

Text and Content

Text Hierarchy

Use opacity to create text hierarchy in dark mode:

  • High emphasis: White at 87% opacity
  • Medium emphasis: White at 60% opacity
  • Disabled: White at 38% opacity

Avoid Pure White Text

Like pure black, pure white (#FFFFFF) can be harsh. Use slightly off-white (#E0E0E0 to #F5F5F5) for body text, reserving brighter white for headings and key information.

Brand Color Adaptation

Your brand's primary color may need adjustment in dark mode. The goal is to maintain brand recognition while ensuring readability:

  • Lighter, less saturated variant for text and small elements
  • Original or slightly adjusted version for large surfaces (buttons, banners)
  • Ensure the adapted color still passes contrast tests

Images and Media

  • Add subtle dark overlays to bright images to blend with the dark UI
  • Consider providing dark variants of illustrations
  • Reduce image brightness slightly to prevent visual shock

Implementation Tips

  • Use CSS custom properties (variables) to switch themes efficiently
  • Test on OLED and LCD screens—dark mode looks very different
  • Respect the user's system preference via prefers-color-scheme
  • Provide a manual toggle as well

Testing

Use Kolr's contrast checker to verify all dark mode color combinations. Export your dark mode palette alongside your light mode palette using the export feature for consistent implementation.

color-naming-conventions.title: Color Naming in Design Systems: A Practical Guide
color-naming-conventions.excerpt: Learn effective color naming conventions for design systems. From semantic naming to numeric scales, create a system your team will actually use.
color-naming-conventions.content:
Why Color Naming Matters

Naming colors seems trivial until your team has "blue", "dark-blue", "new-blue", "blue-v2", and "button-blue" in their codebase. Good naming conventions make your design system scalable, maintainable, and intuitive for everyone who uses it.

Common Naming Approaches

1. Descriptive Names

Using names like "ocean-blue", "forest-green", or "sunset-orange". These are intuitive but don't scale well—what comes after "dark-blue"? "Darker-blue"?

2. Numeric Scales

Using numbers like blue-50, blue-100, blue-200... through blue-900. This is the Tailwind approach and it scales beautifully. Numbers communicate relative lightness without ambiguity.

3. Semantic Names

Using purpose-based names like "color-primary", "color-danger", "color-success". These describe what the color does, not what it looks like.

The Best Approach: Layered Naming

Most successful design systems use a two-layer approach:

Layer 1: Primitive Tokens (Base Colors)

Define your raw colors with neutral, scalable names:

  • blue-50, blue-100, blue-200... blue-900
  • gray-50, gray-100... gray-900
  • red-50, red-100... red-900

Layer 2: Semantic Tokens (Purpose)

Map primitives to purpose-based aliases:

  • color-primary → blue-600
  • color-primary-hover → blue-700
  • color-background → gray-50
  • color-text → gray-900
  • color-danger → red-600

Naming Conventions to Follow

  • Use kebab-case: "color-primary" not "colorPrimary" (in CSS/tokens)
  • Be consistent: Don't mix "bg-" and "background-" prefixes
  • Include state: "color-primary-hover", "color-primary-disabled"
  • Avoid color names in semantic tokens: Don't name it "color-blue"—if you rebrand, you'll have a "color-blue" that's actually green

Dark Mode Naming

Semantic tokens make dark mode trivial. Instead of duplicating colors, just remap:

  • Light: color-background → gray-50
  • Dark: color-background → gray-900

Your components reference "color-background" and automatically adapt.

Practical Example

Export your Kolr palette as CSS variables or JSON tokens, then apply your naming convention. Kolr's export formats give you a clean starting point that you can reorganize into your preferred naming system.

photography-color-grading.title: Photography Color Grading for Designers
photography-color-grading.excerpt: Apply color grading principles from photography to your design work. Learn about color temperature, tonal adjustments, and mood creation.
photography-color-grading.content:
What Is Color Grading?

Color grading is the process of altering and enhancing the color of images to create a specific mood or aesthetic. While it originated in film and photography, the principles apply directly to design—helping you create consistent visual atmospheres across projects.

Color Temperature

Warm Grading

Shifting colors toward yellow/orange creates warmth, nostalgia, and intimacy. Warm grading is common in:

  • Lifestyle and travel photography
  • Food photography (warm tones stimulate appetite)
  • Golden hour and sunset aesthetics

Cool Grading

Shifting toward blue/teal creates distance, professionalism, or moodiness. Cool grading works for:

  • Technology and corporate imagery
  • Night scenes and urban aesthetics
  • Winter and minimalist themes

The Teal and Orange Look

The most popular color grading technique pushes shadows toward teal and highlights toward orange. This creates a cinematic feel because it leverages complementary colors and mimics natural skin tone contrast against cool backgrounds.

How to Achieve It

  • Shift shadow hues toward blue-green (teal)
  • Shift highlight hues toward warm orange
  • Maintain midtone neutrality for natural skin tones

Matte/Film Look

Raising the black point (so shadows never reach pure black) creates a faded, vintage aesthetic. This technique:

  • Reduces contrast for a softer feel
  • Adds a nostalgic, analog quality
  • Works well with desaturated, pastel color palettes

Extracting Palettes from Graded Photos

Color-graded photographs make excellent palette sources because the colors have already been curated for harmony and mood. Use Kolr's image extractor on your favorite graded photos to capture their palettes.

Applying Grading Principles to Design

Consistent Image Treatment

Apply the same color grading to all images in a project. This creates visual cohesion even with photos from different sources.

Palette Derivation

Extract a palette from your graded look and use it for UI elements, typography, and backgrounds. This creates a seamless connection between imagery and interface.

Brand Photography Guidelines

Document your color grading settings as part of your brand guidelines. Include before/after examples and specific adjustment values.

Tools and Workflow

Grade your photos in Lightroom or similar tools, then extract the resulting palette with Kolr. Export in CSS variables to use the exact same colors throughout your web design.

minimalist-color-palettes.title: Creating Minimalist Color Palettes That Speak Volumes
minimalist-color-palettes.excerpt: Less is more in minimalist design. Learn to create powerful palettes with just 2-3 colors and master the art of visual restraint.
minimalist-color-palettes.content:
The Minimalist Color Philosophy

Minimalist design isn't about removing all color—it's about using color with maximum intention. Every color in a minimalist palette must earn its place, serving a clear purpose in the visual hierarchy.

The Two-Color Palette

The most powerful minimalist palettes use just two colors (plus neutrals):

  • A dominant neutral: White, off-white, or very dark (for dark themes)
  • A single accent: One carefully chosen color that draws attention to what matters most

Examples

  • White + cobalt blue: Clean, trustworthy, corporate
  • Off-white + burnt orange: Warm, inviting, artisanal
  • Near-black + electric green: Technical, modern, edgy

The Rule of Three

Most minimalist palettes work with three elements:

  • Background: Your dominant neutral
  • Text: High-contrast reading color
  • Accent: Your single brand/action color

Maximizing Impact with Restraint

Strategic Color Placement

When you use color sparingly, every instance carries weight. A single red button on a white page is impossible to miss. That's the power of restraint.

Whitespace as a Color

In minimalist design, empty space is an active design element. It provides breathing room, creates focus, and lets your limited palette shine.

Typography as Color

Strong typography reduces the need for color. Bold weights, size variation, and typeface contrast create hierarchy without adding hues.

When Minimalism Works Best

  • Content-first websites (blogs, publications)
  • Portfolio and gallery sites
  • Premium and luxury brands
  • Professional services
  • Documentation and tools

When to Add More Color

Minimalism isn't always the answer. Add more colors when:

  • You need to distinguish many categories or data types
  • Your audience expects vibrancy (children, entertainment)
  • The brand personality demands boldness

Building Minimalist Palettes

Start with Kolr's random palette generator, then remove colors until only the essentials remain. Test your reduced palette in context—if it still communicates clearly and looks intentional, you've found your minimalist palette.

color-contrast-for-readability.title: Color Contrast for Maximum Readability: A Technical Deep Dive
color-contrast-for-readability.excerpt: Master the science of readable color combinations. Understand contrast ratios, luminance calculations, and how to choose text colors that work everywhere.
color-contrast-for-readability.content:
The Science of Readability

Reading is a complex visual task that depends heavily on the contrast between text and background. The wrong contrast—too low or even too high—can slow reading speed, increase errors, and cause eye strain.

How Contrast Ratios Work

The WCAG contrast ratio formula compares the relative luminance of two colors:

Ratio = (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05)

Where L1 is the lighter color's luminance and L2 is the darker. The result ranges from 1:1 (no contrast) to 21:1 (black on white).

Relative Luminance

Luminance isn't simply brightness—it accounts for how the human eye perceives different wavelengths. Green contributes 71.5% to perceived luminance, red 21.3%, and blue only 7.2%. This is why yellow text is harder to read than blue text on white backgrounds, despite yellow being "brighter."

Optimal Contrast Ranges

Body Text (14-16px)

Aim for 7:1 to 15:1. WCAG AAA requires 7:1, but going beyond 15:1 (like pure black on pure white) can cause halation—where bright backgrounds seem to bleed into dark text.

Large Text (18px+ or 14px+ bold)

A minimum of 4.5:1 (WCAG AA) works for headings and large display text.

UI Elements

Interactive controls need at least 3:1 contrast against their backgrounds. This includes buttons, form inputs, and focus indicators.

Common Readability Mistakes

  • Gray text on white: Light gray (#999) on white only achieves 2.85:1—far below standards
  • Colored text on colored backgrounds: Two saturated colors can have surprisingly low contrast
  • Thin fonts at low contrast: Thin weights need higher contrast than bold weights
  • Ignoring anti-aliasing: Subpixel rendering can reduce effective contrast by 20-30%

Practical Contrast Guidelines

  • Body text: Use dark gray (#222 to #333) on light backgrounds, not pure black
  • Secondary text: #666 on white achieves exactly 5.74:1—just above AA for normal text
  • Placeholder text: Even dimmed text should maintain readability—use #767676 minimum on white
  • Colored links: Ensure at least 3:1 contrast against surrounding body text

Testing Your Contrast

Use Kolr's contrast checker to test specific color pairs against all WCAG criteria simultaneously. It shows AA and AAA compliance for both normal and large text, letting you make informed decisions quickly.

from-inspiration-to-palette.title: From Inspiration to Palette: A Designer's Complete Workflow
from-inspiration-to-palette.excerpt: Follow a professional workflow from finding color inspiration to creating a polished, production-ready palette. Includes real-world examples and tools.
from-inspiration-to-palette.content:
The Professional Palette Workflow

Creating a color palette isn't a single-step process. Professional designers follow a structured workflow that takes them from initial inspiration to a production-ready color system. Here's how to do it.

Step 1: Gather Inspiration

Sources

  • Photography: Nature, architecture, food, and fashion photos contain proven color harmonies
  • Art: Classical and contemporary art offers masterful color relationships
  • Competitors: Analyze what works (and doesn't) in your industry
  • Trend reports: Pantone, design blogs, and platform-specific trend data
  • Real world: Observe colors in everyday environments—markets, gardens, cityscapes

Collecting

Save inspiration in a dedicated folder or mood board. Capture what draws you to each reference—is it a specific color, a combination, or the overall mood?

Step 2: Extract Raw Colors

Use Kolr's image color extractor to pull colors from your inspiration images. Don't limit yourself to one image—extract from several and look for recurring themes.

Identify Patterns

  • Which hue families appear most often?
  • What's the typical saturation level?
  • Are the palettes warm, cool, or mixed?

Step 3: Refine and Select

Choose Your Core Colors

From your extracted colors, select 3-5 that represent the direction you want. Consider:

  • One dominant color (will be used most)
  • One or two supporting colors
  • One accent color (for highlights and CTAs)

Adjust for Purpose

Raw extracted colors rarely work perfectly out of the box. Adjust:

  • Saturation (increase for digital, decrease for print or subtle use)
  • Lightness (ensure variety across the value range)
  • Consistency (all colors should feel like they belong together)

Step 4: Test for Harmony

Use Kolr's color harmony explorer to verify your choices work together. Check that your palette includes:

  • Sufficient value range (light to dark)
  • A balance of warm and cool tones (if applicable)
  • No unintentional clashes or muddy combinations

Step 5: Verify Accessibility

Before finalizing, test every color combination for contrast:

  • Primary text on each background color
  • CTA button text on button background
  • Link colors against body text
  • Error, warning, and success colors in context

Step 6: Build the Full System

Extend your 3-5 core colors into a complete system:

  • Generate tint/shade scales for each color
  • Define neutral palette (grays with your dominant hue's undertone)
  • Add semantic colors (success, warning, error, info)
  • Create dark mode variants if needed

Step 7: Export and Document

Export your palette using Kolr in CSS variables, Tailwind config, SCSS, or JSON format. Document usage guidelines: which colors for text, backgrounds, borders, interactive elements, and states.

Step 8: Review and Iterate

Apply your palette to actual designs and review:

  • Does it match the intended mood?
  • Is everything readable and accessible?
  • Does it work across different contexts (mobile, desktop, print)?

Great palettes are rarely perfect on the first try. Iterate based on real-world testing and feedback.

What Is the Gradient Generator?

The Gradient Generator is a free online tool that lets you create stunning CSS gradients with full control over colors, direction, and type. Whether you need a subtle background wash for a landing page or a vibrant, eye-catching hero section, this tool gives you pixel-perfect control in seconds.

Gradients are a fundamental element of modern UI design. They add depth, guide the eye, and create visual interest without introducing additional imagery — which means faster page loads and a cleaner aesthetic. From linear gradients that transition left to right, to radial gradients that bloom from a center point, to conic gradients that sweep like a color wheel, the possibilities are virtually limitless.

Designers use this tool for website backgrounds, button highlights, card overlays, social-media banners, and data-visualization accents. Developers love the one-click CSS copy feature that outputs production-ready code for any modern browser.

  • Supports linear, radial, and conic gradient types
  • Add, remove, and reorder color stops
  • Copy clean CSS code with one click
  • Randomize for instant inspiration
toolGradient.howToContent:
How to Use the Gradient Generator

Creating a custom CSS gradient is quick and intuitive. Follow these steps to design, preview, and export your gradient.

  1. Choose a gradient type — Select Linear, Radial, or Conic from the type selector at the top of the tool.
  2. Set the angle or position — For linear gradients, drag the angle slider or type a degree value. For radial and conic gradients, the origin defaults to center.
  3. Pick your colors — Click on a color stop to open the color picker and choose a color. The gradient preview updates in real time.
  4. Add more color stops — Click the Add Color button to introduce additional stops. You can add up to eight colors for complex, multi-tone gradients.
  5. Remove unwanted stops — Click the Remove button next to any color stop you want to delete (minimum two stops required).
  6. Preview the result — The large preview panel shows exactly how the gradient will render on screen.
  7. Randomize — Click Random Gradient for algorithmic inspiration. The tool picks harmonious colors and a random type/angle combination.
  8. Copy the CSS — Click Copy CSS to place the complete gradient declaration on your clipboard, ready to paste into your stylesheet.

Tip: pair gradients with semi-transparent overlays (rgba) to create frosted-glass or duotone effects that are trending in modern web design.

toolColorblind.description: See how your palette looks to people with different types of color vision
